title: War, occupation, and the destruction of Lviv Jewry
summary: The wartime records document how persecution dismantled the community and transformed the city into a site of deportation, forced labor, and murder.

## Occupation and the destruction of communal life

When German forces entered [Lviv](/communities/lviv/records/mention_13c288289ae43386483701e4) in June 1941, they occupied a city whose borders and rulers had changed repeatedly in the preceding years. Soviet forces had taken Lviv in September 1939; Yad Vashem’s account notes that Jewish refugees from western Poland also arrived after that takeover. The German invasion of the Soviet Union brought a new occupation—and immediate violence against the Jews. Yad Vashem reports thousands murdered in pogroms in the first weeks, while the memorial book recounts the German-led plunder, forced labor and persecution that followed. These accounts provide different kinds of evidence: the memorial book preserves the community’s recollection, while Yad Vashem supplies a concise historical overview. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/Microsoft%20Word%20-%206457.pdf))

The attack reached not only people but the places that had embodied communal life. The memorial book says the Germans systematically burned synagogues, including the Golden Rose and the Temple prayer house on Żółkiewska Street; other synagogues were later demolished. The book also records the removal of Jewish cemetery stones for road paving, including at Janowska. These details make the destruction tangible: sacred buildings and memorial stones were turned into material for the occupying regime. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lviv/lvi593.html))

## A council under German command

In July 1941, German authorities created a Jewish council to carry out German orders. The memorial book’s account of the council’s composition says that appointments and additions were completed by July 20, while its broader narrative says the process continued through July 29 and gives an autumn roster. Rather than treating either date as a precise final moment, it is safest to say that the council took shape through appointments over July and was later altered. Among those named were Oswald Kimelman, Edmund Scherzer, Naftali Landau and Shimon Ulam. The record that the [Jewish Council’s composition was finalized](/communities/lviv/records/event_candidate_486b485088e985425f7c483d) thus describes a process, not a single uncontested instant. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lviv/lvi593.html))

The German-imposed [Lviv Jewish Council](/communities/lviv/records/mention_d837739462c40ad1e06412ee) was at once an administrative structure and an instrument of coercion. It handled food distribution, housing, employment and social assistance, but those responsibilities were exercised under German orders and amid extortion, forced labor and escalating violence. The memorial book describes a succession of chairmen: Józef Parnas, arrested and killed after refusing German demands; Adolf Rotfeld, who replaced him; Henryk Landsberg, murdered in September 1942; and Dr. Eberson, killed with other council members in 1943. Yad Vashem likewise dates Parnas’s killing to late October 1941, while the memorial account leaves the arrest to October or November. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lviv/lvi593.html))

The roster links individual lives to the institution’s changing fate. The book names [Dr. Kimelman](/communities/lviv/records/mention_3ba0fefcc564cdc407745124), [Dr. Eberson](/communities/lviv/records/mention_ffbd3eec1707c0a42a4098c3), [Joseph Landsberg](/communities/lviv/records/mention_0afe4914d33413d54406f182), [Shimon Ulam](/communities/lviv/records/mention_6d44d0909b33387109b8de86), [Adolf Rotfeld](/communities/lviv/records/mention_38fb301964051e6a8420dfda), [Osold Kimelman](/communities/lviv/records/mention_1cb3e4c6b3ee8661accf0635), [Edmund Scherzer](/communities/lviv/records/mention_f088ce11b63ec5cc0e7265e4) and [Naftali Landau](/communities/lviv/records/mention_734929356fdcc664bc37368c). It also recalls [Dr. Martzeli Bober](/communities/lviv/records/mention_d27a72f5b96a7e20558fa5f5) and [Dr. Yosef Frans](/communities/lviv/records/mention_b46f7734b6e86fbabce82d87). Its records connect Eberson, Kimelman and Landsberg to the [Ghetto Council](/communities/lviv/records/mention_af3a84a1b463e1e318ca2eda). They do not, however, establish additional family relationships among these men; names and offices should not be mistaken for kinship.

## Ghetto, deportation and Janowska

In November 1941, the Germans confined Lviv’s Jews to a ghetto. The memorial book’s account traces the community’s shrinking numbers through food-card registrations: from about 119,000 in October 1941 to 82,000 in June and July 1942, then sharply down to 36,000 in September. These are registration figures, not a complete census, but they show the scale and speed of loss. Yad Vashem places the ghetto’s creation in November and records deportations to Bełżec in spring 1942, followed by further deportations and killings that summer. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lviv/lvi645.html))

The chronology of individual Aktionen in the records is not always settled. One account places a sudden twelve-hour action on either June 24 or July 8, 1942; the memorial-book passage itself preserves both possibilities, so neither should be asserted as certain. Another record dates a raid on the [Municipal Workshops](/communities/lviv/records/mention_4313c68ca9c4096e98620e2a) to August 13 and says more than 4,000 people were sent to Janowska. Yet the book’s larger chapter dates the August Grossaktion’s beginning to August 10. These may describe related but distinct stages or raids; the evidence does not permit collapsing them into one exact date. A [screening committee at the central reception site](/communities/lviv/records/event_candidate_00f3a12939748d3af0f47085) is mentioned without a date.

[Janowska camp](/communities/lviv/records/mention_bce1477af2526c752c180d16) was more than a forced-labor destination: the US Holocaust Memorial Museum describes it as a transit camp in the 1942 deportations, from which many people were sent to Bełżec or murdered nearby. The memorial book follows council figures and other prisoners into Janowska, including Shimon Ulam, and records [David Frankel](/communities/lviv/records/mention_c7ea932d2620a605a58d5c86) among those active in underground resistance. The wider camp history includes a November 1943 uprising and escape attempt during the camp’s liquidation. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/janowska))

## Cultural life and resistance in hiding

The ghetto’s cultural life was driven underground, but it did not disappear. The memorial book says public lectures, schools, theatre and organized religious activity were forbidden. Small prayer groups met secretly; children studied in private homes; writers and political activists gathered out of sight. Its account names Henryk Graf as an organizer of literary meetings, with Abraham Blatt opening some evenings, actress Hoffman reading biblical texts and poet Maurycy Szymel sometimes sharing his work. The book recalls a series of [literary evenings](/communities/lviv/records/event_candidate_28e9c8c59e5853e9b7bbe2b7) in 1942–1943, while also describing earlier gatherings in council offices. The difference in framing suggests a clandestine practice that shifted over time, rather than a single event with one clear starting date. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lviv/lvi645.html))

Resistance also took forms beyond armed revolt. The book describes young council employees secretly learning military skills and weapons handling in late 1942, though no organized unit resulted. It records attempts to escape toward the forests, an illegal underground newspaper, and clandestine cultural meetings. These efforts existed amid severe danger and often ended in capture or death. The account of Lviv’s clandestine life is not a story of safety or easy defiance; it is evidence of people trying to preserve thought, solidarity and agency under conditions designed to extinguish them. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lviv/lvi693.html))

The destruction of Lviv’s Jewry was carried out in stages: occupation violence, coercive administration, confinement, deportation and murder. The memorial book preserves names, remembered episodes and the community’s own account of this progression. Independent records from Yad Vashem and the US Holocaust Memorial Museum confirm key elements—the ghetto’s establishment, deportations, and Janowska’s role—while also making clear that the fate of the Jews of Lviv extended beyond the city and its council. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/Microsoft%20Word%20-%206457.pdf))
